summary: This chapter is about germs and how to keep clients and yourself safe from them. You will learn the main types of microorganisms and the three levels of germ control. The exam often asks which level fits which tool or situation.

Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites can all cause problems in a salon or spa. Bacteria are single cells, and some form round, rod, or spiral shapes. Viruses are much smaller and need a living host to multiply, so a disinfectant cannot treat a virus that is already inside a person.

Sanitation, disinfection, and sterilization are three steps up a ladder. Sanitation only lowers the number of germs on a clean surface. Disinfection kills most germs on hard, nonporous items, and sterilization kills every living microbe, including spores. A tool must be cleaned before it is disinfected, because dirt blocks the disinfectant.

Porous items such as cotton pads, wooden sticks, and emery boards cannot be disinfected, so they are used once and thrown away. Blood and body fluids are treated as possibly infectious on every client. Handwashing, gloves, and clean linens are everyday habits that help prevent the spread of infection.

concepts.definition: The lowest level of germ control. Washing with soap and water lowers the number of germs on a surface but does not kill them all.
concepts.tip: Sanitize = clean. It is the first step, not the last.

concepts.definition: A level above sanitation that kills most germs on hard, nonporous surfaces such as metal tools and countertops. A product must be used with its label directions, including contact time.
concepts.tip: Disinfect after cleaning, and keep the item wet for the full contact time.

concepts.definition: The highest level. It destroys all microbial life, including spores. Medical settings use an autoclave to do it.
concepts.tip: Sterile = nothing alive is left.

concepts.definition: Items with tiny holes that soak up liquid, such as cotton pads, emery boards, and wooden spatulas. They cannot be disinfected.
concepts.tip: If you cannot disinfect it, use it once and throw it away.

concepts.definition: Treating all blood and body fluids as possibly infectious, no matter who the client is. This includes wearing gloves and cleaning up spills safely.
concepts.tip: Assume every client could carry something.

concepts.definition: Cocci are round, bacilli are rod-shaped, and spirilla are spiral. Staphylococci grow in clusters and are linked to many skin infections.
concepts.tip: Round = cocci, rod = bacilli, spiral = spirilla.

concepts.definition: Workplace rules require protecting workers from contact with infected blood. Exposure after a cut should be handled by washing, bandaging, and following the workplace plan.
concepts.tip: Cut during a service: stop, glove up, clean, and cover the area.

source.org: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030, issued 1991, revised 2001)

points: The order is clean first, then disinfect. A dirty tool cannot be disinfected well.
Only sterilization kills spores.
Single-use porous items go in the trash after one client.
Viruses need a living host; antibiotics do not work on them.
Wash your hands before and after every client.

compare.title: Three levels of germ control
rows: Washing a brush with soap and water
Kills most germs on hard surfaces
Soaking clean metal tweezers in a disinfectant

summary: This chapter explains how the body is built and how the skin works. It starts with cells and works up to organs and body systems. The exam also asks about skin layers and the muscles and nerves of the face.

The cell is the basic unit of life. Cells of the same kind form a tissue, tissues form an organ such as the skin, and organs working together form a body system. The skin is the body's largest organ and protects against germs, water loss, and the sun.

The skin has three main parts. The epidermis is the thin outer layer with no blood vessels, and it makes new cells that move upward and shed. The dermis lies beneath it and holds blood vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles. Under the dermis, the subcutaneous layer stores fat and cushions the body.

Melanin is the pigment made by melanocytes in the deepest layer of the epidermis. It gives skin its color and helps absorb UV light. On the face, the trigeminal nerve carries feeling, and the facial nerve moves the muscles of expression.

concepts.definition: The basic unit of life. Each cell takes in nutrients, makes energy, and divides to make new cells.
concepts.tip: Cells, then tissues, then organs, then systems.

concepts.definition: The outer layer of skin. It has no blood vessels and constantly renews itself as cells move up and shed from the surface.
concepts.tip: Epi means upon. It is the part you can see.

concepts.definition: The thicker layer under the epidermis. It holds blood vessels, nerves, oil and sweat glands, hair follicles, and collagen.
concepts.tip: Blood vessels, nerves, and glands are in the dermis.

concepts.definition: The fatty layer below the dermis. It cushions the body, saves energy, and holds heat.
concepts.tip: Sub means below the skin.

concepts.definition: The pigment that gives skin and hair color. It is made by melanocytes and helps shield deeper cells from UV light.
concepts.tip: More melanin means more natural sun protection, not full protection.

concepts.definition: The chief sensory nerve of the face. It carries feelings such as touch and pain from the face to the brain.
concepts.tip: Trigeminal = tri means three branches of feeling.

concepts.definition: The motor nerve that moves the muscles of facial expression, such as smiling and frowning.
concepts.tip: Facial nerve = facial movement.

points: The epidermis has no blood supply; the dermis does.
Collagen and elastin in the dermis give firmness and stretch.
Melanocytes make melanin.
The trigeminal nerve senses; the facial nerve moves.
Skin protects, senses, regulates heat, and holds in water.

summary: This chapter covers what can go wrong with the skin. You will learn which glands make oil and sweat, how to name a lesion, and which conditions are contagious. A key skill is knowing when a condition is outside your scope and needs a doctor.

Sebaceous glands make oil called sebum, and sudoriferous glands make sweat. When a pore clogs with oil and dead cells, a comedone forms. An open one is a blackhead and a closed one is a whitehead. Acne can then become red bumps and pus-filled spots.

Lesions are grouped as primary or secondary. Primary lesions, such as macules, papules, vesicles, and pustules, appear first on the skin. Secondary lesions, such as crusts, scales, and scars, develop later or from changes in a primary one.

Some conditions spread from person to person. Ringworm (tinea), impetigo, and scabies are contagious, so an esthetician does not treat them and sends the client to a physician. Skin growths and cancers need medical evaluation. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, and melanoma is the most dangerous.

concepts.definition: Oil glands attached to hair follicles. They make sebum, which keeps skin soft and helps protect it.
concepts.tip: Sebaceous = sebum = oil.

concepts.definition: Sweat glands that help cool the body and remove some waste through the skin.
concepts.tip: Sudoriferous = sweat.

concepts.definition: Changes that appear first on the skin. Examples are macule (flat spot), papule (small raised bump), vesicle (fluid-filled blister), and pustule (pus-filled bump).
concepts.tip: Primary lesions are the first to show.

concepts.definition: Changes that develop later on the skin. Examples are crust (dried fluid), scale (flakes), and scar (new tissue after injury).
concepts.tip: Secondary lesions come after something else.

concepts.definition: Tinea (ringworm, a fungus), impetigo (bacterial, honey-colored crusts), and scabies (a mite) pass to others easily. Do not provide services; refer the client.
concepts.tip: Contagious means refer, do not treat.

concepts.definition: Dark patches where the skin makes extra melanin. Melasma and age spots are examples, and sun exposure can make them worse.
concepts.tip: Hyper means more color; hypo means less.

concepts.definition: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common and rarely spreads. Squamous cell carcinoma is next. Melanoma is the most dangerous because it can spread.
concepts.tip: Any changing mole goes to a doctor.

points: An esthetician does not diagnose or treat disease.
Primary lesions appear first; secondary lesions follow.
Refer contagious or unclear conditions to a physician.
Melanoma is the most dangerous skin cancer.
A blackhead is an open comedone; a whitehead is closed.

summary: This chapter covers the basics of hair, electricity, and workplace safety. These topics are linked because estheticians use electrical devices and chemicals near clients. The exam asks simple definitions and safe habits.

A strand of hair has three layers. The cuticle is the outer layer of overlapping scales, the cortex is the middle layer that gives strength and color, and the medulla is the center, which is not always present. The hair grows from a follicle, and the growth cycle has three phases. Anagen is growth, catagen is a short transition, and telogen is rest.

Electricity is measured with a few basic units. The volt measures the pressure pushing the current, the ampere measures the amount of current, and the ohm measures resistance. A conductor lets current flow easily, and an insulator blocks it. Direct current flows one way, while alternating current switches direction.

Safe equipment use means keeping cords and plugs in good shape, keeping cords, plugs, and outlets dry, and not overloading outlets. A fuse or circuit breaker stops the current if there is too much. A Safety Data Sheet explains the hazards of each chemical, and chemicals should be kept in labeled, closed containers.

concepts.definition: The cuticle is the outer protective layer, the cortex is the middle layer with strength and pigment, and the medulla is the center core.
concepts.tip: Cuticle outside, cortex middle, medulla middle-most.

concepts.definition: The active growth phase of the hair cycle, when the hair bulb makes new hair. Most scalp hairs are in this phase at any time.
concepts.tip: Anagen = active.

concepts.definition: A short transition phase when growth stops and the follicle shrinks.
concepts.tip: Catagen = changing.

concepts.definition: The resting phase before the hair sheds and a new hair begins.
concepts.tip: Telogen = tired, resting.

concepts.definition: A volt measures electrical pressure, an ampere measures the strength of current, and an ohm measures resistance to flow.
concepts.tip: Volt = push, amp = amount, ohm = obstacle.

concepts.definition: A conductor, such as metal or water, lets electricity pass. An insulator, such as rubber or plastic, blocks it.
concepts.tip: Rubber protects; water carries.

concepts.definition: A document from the maker that lists a chemical's hazards, first aid, and safe handling. A salon should keep one for each hazardous chemical product it uses.
concepts.tip: Question about a chemical? Look at the SDS.

points: Hair growth order is anagen, catagen, telogen.
Never touch devices or plugs with wet hands, and keep cords, plugs, and outlets dry.
A circuit breaker or fuse stops too much current.
Keep chemicals in labeled containers and never mix them.
Use the SDS for hazards and first aid.

summary: This chapter explains what to do before the service starts. A good consultation helps you choose safe products and treatments and builds trust with the client. You will also learn skin types and the Fitzpatrick scale.

The client fills out an intake form and then talks with you about health history, allergies, medicines, current products, and goals. Look for conditions that could make a service unsafe. If a client has a medical concern, you refer them to a physician instead of diagnosing it. Keep records private and update them at each visit.

Skin types describe how the skin behaves. Normal skin is balanced, dry skin lacks oil, oily skin makes extra oil, and combination skin is oily in the T-zone and drier on the cheeks. Sensitive skin reacts easily. Dehydrated skin lacks water, which is different from lacking oil, and any skin type can be dehydrated.

The Fitzpatrick scale groups skin by how it reacts to sun, from Type I, which burns easily, to Type VI, which almost never burns. It helps you choose treatments and sun advice. Tools like a magnifying lamp and Wood's lamp help you look at the skin closely.

concepts.definition: A form that records contact details, health history, allergies, medicines, and skin care habits before a first service.
concepts.tip: Complete the intake form before the first service.

concepts.definition: A reason that a service should not be done because it could harm the client. Examples include active infection or a recent sunburn.
concepts.tip: When in doubt, skip it and refer.

concepts.definition: What an esthetician is allowed to do. It does not include diagnosing disease or prescribing medicine.
concepts.tip: Describe, do not diagnose.

concepts.definition: Skin that is oily in the T-zone (forehead, nose, chin) and normal or dry on the cheeks.
concepts.tip: T-zone oily = combination.

concepts.definition: Skin that lacks water. It can look tight and dull, and it can be oily at the same time.
concepts.tip: Dry lacks oil; dehydrated lacks water.

concepts.definition: A six-type scale that groups skin by how it reacts to sun. Type I always burns and rarely tans; Type VI almost never burns and has deep pigment.
concepts.tip: Low number burns fast; high number burns slowly.

concepts.definition: A black-light device that makes some skin conditions and oil levels show up under different colors in a dim room.
concepts.tip: Wood's lamp = look under black light.

points: Always do the consultation before touching the skin.
Refer medical concerns to a physician.
Dehydration is about water, dryness is about oil.
Fitzpatrick Type I burns most easily; Type VI least.
Keep client records private.

summary: This chapter walks through the facial from start to finish and the ways to exfoliate. The exam asks about the correct order of steps and which massage movement is which. You will also compare chemical and mechanical exfoliation.

A basic facial begins with a consultation, then removes makeup and cleanses the skin. Next comes skin analysis, exfoliation, and steam if suitable. Extractions may follow, then massage, a mask, and finally toner, moisturizer, and sunscreen. Keeping that order helps in answering sequence questions.

Massage uses five classic movements. Effleurage is light gliding, petrissage is kneading, friction is firm circular pressure, tapotement is tapping, and vibration is fine shaking. Effleurage is often used to begin and end the massage because it calms the client.

Exfoliation removes dead surface cells. Chemical exfoliants such as alpha hydroxy acids and beta hydroxy acids loosen the bonds between cells. Mechanical exfoliation, such as scrubs, brushes, or microdermabrasion, rubs the cells off. Steam softens skin, but it should be limited for clients with couperose skin or rosacea.

concepts.definition: Cleanse, analyze, exfoliate, steam if suitable, extract if needed, massage, mask, then tone, moisturize, and protect with sunscreen.
concepts.tip: Clean first, protect last.

concepts.definition: A light, gliding massage stroke. It is relaxing and is used to start and end a massage.
concepts.tip: Effleurage = easy gliding.

concepts.definition: A kneading movement that lifts and squeezes the tissue. It helps with circulation in the muscles.
concepts.tip: Petrissage = pinch and knead like dough.

concepts.definition: A tapping or drumming movement, done lightly on the face. It is stimulating.
concepts.tip: Tapotement = tap.

concepts.definition: AHAs, such as glycolic and lactic acid, are water-soluble and work on the skin surface. BHA, salicylic acid, is oil-soluble and can reach into pores.
concepts.tip: A for the surface, B for oily pores.

concepts.definition: Removing dead cells by rubbing or abrasion, such as with a scrub, brush, or microdermabrasion.
concepts.tip: Mechanical = physical rubbing.

concepts.definition: Warm moisture used to soften the skin and the debris in pores before extractions. Keep it short and at a safe distance.
concepts.tip: Skip or shorten steam for couperose or rosacea skin.

points: The five massage movements are effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement, and vibration.
Sunscreen should end every daytime facial.
Do not use strong exfoliation on irritated or sunburned skin.
Wash hands and wear gloves before extractions.
Avoid mechanical scrubs over active acne lesions.

compare.title: Chemical vs. mechanical exfoliation
rows: Too much rubbing can scratch skin

summary: This chapter covers temporary hair removal and services for the eyebrows and eyelashes. The main ideas are the difference between removing hair at the root and at the surface, and how to wax safely. Many questions ask about contraindications.

Epilation removes the whole hair, including the root. Waxing, tweezing, and threading are examples. Depilation removes hair only at the surface of the skin, and shaving and depilatory creams are examples. Hair removed at the root takes longer to grow back.

For both soft wax and hard wax, the wax is applied in the direction of growth. Soft wax is removed with a strip and hard wax is lifted off by hand, and both are pulled back against growth, close and parallel to the skin, to reduce pain and breakage. Test the wax temperature first and never double-dip a stick. Do not wax skin that is sunburned, broken, or irritated, or skin treated with certain medications.

Brow shaping uses tweezers or wax to remove stray hairs and follows the natural arch. Tinting adds color to lashes or brows and requires a patch test first, because dyes can cause allergic reactions. The FDA has not approved any color additive for dyeing lashes or brows, and some states restrict the service, so check your state board's rules. Protect the eyes during any lash or brow service.

concepts.definition: Removal of the hair along with the root. Waxing, tweezing, and threading are examples.
concepts.tip: Epilation = the root comes out.

concepts.definition: Removal of hair only at the skin surface. Shaving and depilatory creams are examples.
concepts.tip: Depilation = surface only.

concepts.definition: Spread wax in the direction of hair growth and remove the strip against growth, pulled parallel to the skin.
concepts.tip: On with the growth, off against it.

concepts.definition: Hard wax hardens by itself and is lifted off without a strip. Soft wax is spread thinly and removed with a cloth or paper strip.
concepts.tip: Hard wax needs no strip.

concepts.definition: A small test of a product on the client's skin to check for an allergic reaction before a full service, such as eyelash tinting. It is done 24 to 48 hours before, depending on the product maker's directions.
concepts.tip: Always test the tint first.

concepts.definition: Sunburn, open cuts, rashes, and skin thinned by some medications. Waxing in these cases can tear or injure the skin.
concepts.tip: Fragile or irritated skin means no wax.

concepts.definition: After waxing, avoid heat, sun, and heavy products on the area for a day. A soothing, clean product can calm the skin.
concepts.tip: Keep it cool, clean, and covered from sun.

points: Never double-dip a wax stick.
Wear gloves when waxing and dispose of used strips.
Test wax temperature on your own wrist first.
A patch test is needed before lash or brow tint.
Stop if the client reports burning or heavy irritation.

summary: This chapter covers makeup color, product safety, sun protection, and the main skin care ingredients. The exam often checks the color wheel, hygiene with makeup tools, and what each ingredient group does.

The primary colors are red, yellow, and blue. Mixing two primaries makes a secondary color: orange, green, or violet. Complementary colors sit opposite one another on the wheel, so they cancel each other when mixed. Green neutralizes redness, and yellow-toned products soften violet tones.

Makeup hygiene protects clients from infection. Use a clean spatula to remove product from a container, never dip an applicator straight into it, and never share or reuse applicators on different clients. Disposable applicators should be used once, and brushes should be cleaned and disinfected between clients.

Skin care ingredients fall into groups by purpose. Humectants draw water into the skin, occlusives form a layer that holds water in, and emollients soften. Broad-spectrum sunscreen protects against both UVA and UVB rays, and SPF mainly rates UVB protection. Daily use of sunscreen helps slow visible aging caused by the sun.

concepts.definition: Red, yellow, and blue. They cannot be made by mixing other colors.
concepts.tip: Red, yellow, blue make everything else.

concepts.definition: Colors directly opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green. They neutralize each other when mixed.
concepts.tip: Opposite colors cancel.

concepts.definition: An ingredient that attracts water to the skin. Glycerin and hyaluronic acid are common examples.
concepts.tip: Humectant = water magnet.

concepts.definition: An ingredient that forms a barrier on the skin to hold in moisture, such as petrolatum or beeswax.
concepts.tip: Occlusive = a lid on moisture.

concepts.definition: An ingredient that softens and smooths the skin by filling gaps between skin cells. Plant oils and some butters are examples.
concepts.tip: Emollient = softener.

concepts.definition: A sunscreen that protects against both UVA rays (mainly aging) and UVB rays (mainly burning). SPF mainly shows protection from UVB.
concepts.tip: Broad spectrum means both UVA and UVB.

concepts.definition: Use a clean spatula for product, single-use applicators for each client, and disinfect brushes between clients. Never put an applicator back into the container.
concepts.tip: Scoop, do not dip.

points: Green cancels redness; yellow softens violet.
Never share makeup applicators between clients.
Sunscreen should be applied daily and reapplied after sweating or swimming.
Humectants pull water in; occlusives hold it in.
Check for ingredient allergies before applying products.
